title: Wrist Drop -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Wrist drop is a disabling neuromuscular condition resulting from injury to the radial nerve, leading to loss of wrist, finger, and thumb extension. Affected individuals typically demonstrate wrist and finger flexion at rest, accompanied by weakness and variable sensory deficits involving the dorsal hand and posterior forearm. Etiologies include humeral shaft fractures, compressive neuropathies such as prolonged external pressure, entrapment syndromes, metabolic deficiencies, autoimmune neuropathies, and iatrogenic injury. Pathophysiology reflects denervation of the extensor musculature, with severity influenced by the level, mechanism, and duration of nerve injury. Prognosis varies widely, ranging from spontaneous recovery in neurapraxia to incomplete functional return in cases of axonal loss or nerve transection.

title: Wrist Drop -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity equips clinicians with comprehensive knowledge to evaluate and manage wrist drop using evidence-based approaches. Participants learn to perform focused neurologic examinations, interpret electrodiagnostic studies, and utilize imaging to localize radial nerve lesions and determine injury severity. Instruction emphasizes appropriate selection of conservative therapies, including splinting and rehabilitation, and the indications for surgical exploration or repair. The activity highlights the role of interprofessional collaboration among clinicians, physical and occupational therapists, neurologists, and surgeons to coordinate timely diagnosis, optimize functional recovery, and reduce long-term disability. Effective team-based communication supports individualized treatment planning, improves patient adherence, and enhances overall outcomes.

title: Wrist Drop -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Identify the signs and symptoms of wrist drop, noting underlying causes to direct timely and effective management. Differentiate proximal from distal radial nerve lesions causing wrist drop based on neurological examination and diagnostic testing. Implement evidence-based management strategies for wrist drop, incorporating immobilization, rehabilitation, surgical referral when indicated, and patient education to optimize functional recovery. Collaborate with the interprofessional team to educate, treat, and monitor patients with wrist drop to improve functional and overall health outcomes. title: Wrist Drop -- Introduction
content: Wrist drop is a disabling clinical condition resulting from dysfunction of the radial nerve, a major peripheral nerve that provides motor innervation to the extensor muscles of the wrist and fingers and sensory innervation to the dorsum of the hand. The extensor mechanism plays a critical role in hand positioning during grasp and functional activities. Therefore, radial nerve palsy results in substantial impairment of hand function.

title: Wrist Drop -- Introduction
content: Radial nerve injury causes loss of wrist and digital extension, producing the characteristic posture of a flaccid, flexed hand when the forearm is held horizontally. Etiologies encompass traumatic causes such as humeral shaft fractures and penetrating injuries, as well as nontraumatic causes, including prolonged external compression (eg, Saturday night palsy). Systemic and metabolic disorders, such as lead toxicity and vasculitic neuropathies, also contribute to radial nerve dysfunction. Management is guided by the underlying etiology and severity of nerve injury. Treatment ranges from conservative measures, such as splinting, rehabilitation, and pharmacologic therapy, to surgical interventions, including nerve exploration, repair, or tendon transfer for severe or persistent deficits. [1]

title: Wrist Drop -- Etiology
content: Etiologies of wrist drop are diverse but most commonly involve trauma or external compression of the radial nerve. Radial nerve compression may occur at multiple points along its course, with the spiral groove of the humerus representing the most frequent site. Prolonged external pressure at this location, classically termed “Saturday night palsy,” produces a conduction block and subsequent motor weakness. Radial nerve palsy is also a well-recognized complication of humeral shaft fractures, reflecting the nerve's close anatomical relationship with the spiral groove.

title: Wrist Drop -- Etiology
content: At the level of the radial head and lateral epicondyle, the radial nerve bifurcates into the posterior interosseous nerve (PIN), a purely motor branch, and the superficial radial sensory nerve. Compression in this region produces distinct clinical syndromes, including PIN, radial tunnel (RTS), and Wartenberg syndromes. [2] PIN syndrome is characterized by weakness of finger and thumb extension without sensory deficits because the PIN contains no sensory fibers. The most common site of entrapment lies within the supinator muscle at the Arcade of Frohse. Wartenberg syndrome is a compression neuropathy of the superficial radial sensory branch near the radial head and typically presents with sensory disturbances without motor weakness. Therefore, true wrist drop does not occur. [3]

title: Wrist Drop -- Etiology
content: RTS, also known as “supinator syndrome,” is often confused with PIN syndrome but represents a distinct clinical entity. The radial tunnel constitutes an anatomical space extending from the radiocapitellar joint to the distal edge of the supinator muscle. [4] RTS most often involves irritation of the radial nerve at anatomical sites similar to those implicated in PIN syndrome. However, the condition presents primarily as deep, aching pain in the proximal forearm without objective motor weakness. Pain-related inhibition may limit wrist or finger extension, but the underlying mechanism is neural irritation rather than true motor compression. [5] RTS may mimic lateral epicondylitis but can be differentiated by tenderness localized 3 to 5 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle.

title: Wrist Drop -- Etiology
content: Noncompressive causes of wrist drop should be considered in atypical or multifocal presentations. Cervical radiculopathy involving C7 or C8 nerve roots may present with wrist or finger drop and should be included in the differential diagnosis. [6] Systemic and metabolic disorders, although less common, represent clinically important etiologies. Vasculitic neuropathies, including polyarteritis nodosa and vasculitis associated with antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, can produce focal radial nerve injury. [7]

title: Wrist Drop -- Etiology
content: Connective tissue diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus, may manifest as wrist drop within mononeuritis multiplex, characterized by acute, painful, asymmetric sensorimotor deficits. [8] Nutritional deficiencies, including thiamine deficiency, may rarely induce focal neuropathies in chronic alcoholism or malnutrition. [9] Heavy metal toxicity, particularly lead poisoning, remains a relevant global cause of radial nerve dysfunction. [10]

title: Wrist Drop -- Epidemiology
content: The incidence of radial nerve palsy in the United States (US) is approximately 2.9 cases per 100,000 persons per year. [11] Global incidence varies by geographic region and population characteristics. In the United Kingdom, the annual incidence of radial neuropathy is estimated at 2.97 per 100,000 in men and 1.42 per 100,000 in women, with the highest rates observed among men aged 75 to 84 years. [12]

title: Wrist Drop -- Epidemiology
content: Radial nerve injuries represent approximately 15% of upper extremity peripheral nerve injuries in the US. The mean age at presentation is 38, with men affected about twice as often as women. [13] Traumatic etiologies are common. A recent meta-analysis reported radial nerve palsy in approximately 12.2% of patients with humeral shaft fractures. [14] The incidence is lower in pediatric populations, with radial nerve palsy occurring in approximately 4.3% of children with humeral shaft fractures. [15]

title: Wrist Drop -- Pathophysiology
content: The pathophysiology of wrist drop involves disruption of radial nerve conduction caused by trauma, compression, entrapment, or systemic nerve injury. Mechanical insults along the nerve’s course, most commonly at the spiral groove of the humerus, within the radial tunnel, or at the Arcade of Frohse, produce focal demyelination and conduction block. Prolonged or severe compression may result in axonal degeneration, leading to more profound and persistent motor deficits. Severity and reversibility of wrist drop depend on the extent of nerve injury, ranging from transient neurapraxia to axonotmesis or neurotmesis. Wrist drop occurring as part of mononeuritis multiplex typically results from axonal injury mediated by immunologic, infectious, paraneoplastic, or inflammatory processes that compromise nerve perfusion and integrity. [16]

title: Wrist Drop -- History and Physical
content: Radial nerve injuries produce characteristic historical and physical examination findings that vary according to the anatomical level of injury. Common presenting symptoms include pain, weakness, and paresthesia, with patterns of motor and sensory deficits reflecting the site of nerve involvement. Proximal radial nerve lesions involving the axilla or upper arm often result from trauma, such as crutch use, shoulder dislocation, or direct injury. Physical examination demonstrates weakness of the triceps, brachioradialis, and wrist and finger extensors, accompanied by sensory loss over the posterior arm, posterior forearm, and dorsum of the hand. Triceps involvement is specific to very proximal lesions and helps distinguish them from more distal injuries.

title: Wrist Drop -- History and Physical
content: The spiral groove of the mid-humerus is the most common site of radial nerve injury, frequently associated with humeral shaft fractures or external compression, classically termed “Saturday night palsy.” Although historically linked to prolonged compression following alcohol intoxication, many cases occur during sleep, with the arm compressed against the patient or another person. Examination typically shows preserved triceps strength, weakness of wrist and finger extension consistent with wrist drop, brachioradialis weakness, and sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand, particularly in the thumb web space.

title: Wrist Drop -- History and Physical
content: Lesions at the level of the elbow or radial tunnel may result from repetitive forearm movements or fractures of the proximal radius. These lesions present with distinct clinical patterns. Wartenberg syndrome involves compression of the superficial radial sensory nerve and often follows repetitive pronation–supination or external compression from objects such as tight wristbands, casts, or handcuffs. Clinical presentation includes numbness or paresthesia along the dorsoradial forearm extending toward the anatomic snuffbox without associated motor weakness.

title: Wrist Drop -- History and Physical
content: PIN syndrome produces weakness of finger and thumb extension without sensory deficits. Wrist drop may be less pronounced in PIN syndrome because the extensor carpi radialis longus branches proximal to the elbow. RTS presents with deep, aching pain over the lateral proximal forearm, worsened by resisted supination or middle finger extension. Pain-related limitation may impair wrist and finger extension, but objective motor weakness and sensory loss are absent. [16]

title: Wrist Drop -- Evaluation
content: Evaluation of wrist drop begins with a detailed history and physical examination aimed at localizing the site of radial nerve injury using characteristic motor and sensory findings. Careful neurologic assessment is essential to distinguish peripheral radial nerve lesions from proximal etiologies. Electrodiagnostic testing, including nerve conduction studies and needle electromyography (EMG), complements the neurologic evaluation and helps confirm the diagnosis and localize the lesion. EMG helps differentiate radial nerve entrapment from mimicking conditions, such as cervical radiculopathy (particularly C7), brachial plexopathy, and mononeuritis multiplex. [16] When generalized or systemic neuropathy is suspected, targeted laboratory testing and inflammatory markers should be obtained in accordance with the clinical differential diagnosis.

title: Wrist Drop -- Evaluation
content: Plain radiography is indicated when trauma is suspected to evaluate for fractures, particularly of the humerus, that may be associated with radial nerve injury. High-resolution ultrasound is increasingly utilized due to its cost-effectiveness, accessibility, and utility for dynamic peripheral nerve evaluation. High-resolution ultrasound identifies structural abnormalities, such as nerve enlargement, constriction, torsion, and fascicular disruption, and is particularly useful for detecting compressive lesions, including lipomas and ganglion cysts, which may influence surgical planning. [17]

title: Wrist Drop -- Evaluation
content: Small case series demonstrate the value of ultrasound in detecting radial nerve swelling at the spiral groove in both traumatic and nontraumatic neuropathies. [18] [19] Magnetic resonance imaging, including magnetic resonance neurography, evaluates suspected nerve compression or injury, particularly in the brachial plexus or proximal nerve segments. Although evidence supporting magnetic resonance imaging for distal peripheral radial nerve lesions is limited, advances in magnetic resonance neurography have improved visualization through high soft-tissue contrast and customizable imaging protocols for specific anatomic regions. [20]

title: Wrist Drop -- Treatment / Management
content: Managing wrist drop is guided by the severity, chronicity, and underlying etiology of radial nerve injury, with the primary goal of restoring upper extremity function. Initial treatment is typically conservative. Dorsal wrist extension splints, with or without dynamic finger extension components, support functional hand positioning and improve activities of daily living. Early splinting enhances hand function and prevents secondary complications such as flexion contractures. [2] [16]

title: Wrist Drop -- Treatment / Management
content: Proper immobilization is critical for humeral shaft fractures complicated by radial nerve palsy in the acute setting. A modified coaptation splint stabilizes the fracture while maintaining appropriate wrist positioning and minimizing further nerve injury. [21] Nonsurgical management is generally preferred for closed, low-grade injuries because spontaneous recovery is common. Severe injuries, including nerve transection, laceration, or high-grade contusion, are unlikely to resolve without intervention and are best managed with surgical exploration.

title: Wrist Drop -- Treatment / Management
content: The optimal timing of surgical intervention remains debated. However, evidence indicates that exploration within approximately 3 weeks of injury yields higher rates of full functional recovery compared with delayed or expectant management. [1] Early surgical exploration permits definitive identification and repair of severe injuries that may otherwise be missed but requires consideration of operative risks, including surgical morbidity and potential iatrogenic nerve injury.

title: Wrist Drop -- Treatment / Management
content: Management of nontraumatic causes of wrist drop should target the underlying pathology. Immunologically mediated radial neuropathies, such as those associated with mixed cryoglobulinemia, may respond rapidly to immunomodulatory therapies, including rituximab. [22] Wrist drop resulting from nutritional deficiencies should be treated with targeted supplementation to correct the specific deficit. Persistent or irreversible motor deficits may be addressed with tendon transfer procedures to restore functional wrist and finger extension.

title: Wrist Drop -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnosis of wrist drop includes the following conditions: C7 radiculopathy Lateral epicondylitis De Quervain tenosynovitis Posterior cord lesions Extensor tendon injuries Multiple sclerosis Vasculitic neuropathy Diabetic polyneuropathy Cerebral cortical infarcts

content: These conditions can cause motor weakness, sensory deficits, or upper-extremity functional impairment, which may mimic radial nerve injury. Accurate diagnosis requires careful correlation of clinical history, physical examination, and targeted diagnostic testing to localize the lesion and identify the underlying etiology.

title: Wrist Drop -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis of wrist drop depends on the mechanism, severity, and anatomical location of radial nerve injury. Acute compressive neuropathies, such as Saturday night palsy, generally carry an excellent prognosis. Most patients achieve complete recovery within 3 to 4 months, particularly when initial weakness is mild and electrodiagnostic studies demonstrate conduction block without evidence of axonal loss. [23]

title: Wrist Drop -- Prognosis
content: In humeral shaft fractures, prognosis is determined primarily by the extent of nerve injury rather than fracture management. Evidence indicates a high rate of spontaneous recovery regardless of operative or nonoperative fracture treatment. Results from a retrospective cohort study of humeral shaft fractures complicated by radial nerve palsy showed that spontaneous nerve recovery occurred in 91% of cases, and operative fixation did not significantly affect outcomes. [24] Similarly, a systematic review reported a spontaneous recovery rate of 77.2% in nonoperatively treated individuals, whereas those who failed conservative treatment and underwent nerve exploration approximately 8 weeks after injury achieved a recovery rate of 68.1%.

title: Wrist Drop -- Prognosis
content: Early surgical intervention may improve outcomes in selected patients, particularly those with open fractures, high-energy trauma, or suspected nerve transection. Functional recovery rates approaching 88% have been reported when surgical repair occurs within 3 weeks of injury. [1] Predictors of poorer outcomes include advanced age, proximal nerve involvement, nerve discontinuity, and delayed treatment. Complete recovery may require up to 1 year, even with appropriate management, often necessitating prolonged rehabilitation. Persistent deficits may be addressed with tendon transfer procedures or adaptive strategies to restore functional hand use.

title: Wrist Drop -- Complications
content: Potential complications of untreated or inadequately managed wrist drop include permanent loss of motor function, progressive joint stiffness, and muscle atrophy. Persistent inability to extend the wrist and fingers significantly impairs hand function, reduces grip strength, and limits performance of activities of daily living, particularly in severe injuries or cases of incomplete neurologic recovery. Chronic denervation of the radial nerve produces marked atrophy of the extensor compartment of the forearm, further restricting functional outcomes and increasing long-term disability. [25]

title: Wrist Drop -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Prevention of wrist drop requires minimizing risk factors related to trauma, prolonged compression, and repetitive overuse. Avoidance of sustained pressure on the upper arm and forearm, including certain sleeping positions, improper crutch use, and tight clothing, braces, or accessories, reduces the risk of radial nerve injury. Education on proper ergonomics, activity modification, and scheduled rest breaks mitigates cumulative nerve stress. Prompt medical evaluation is recommended for new-onset weakness, sensory changes, or persistent upper extremity pain. Early recognition and intervention prevent the progression of nerve injury and reduce the likelihood of permanent functional impairment. [25]

title: Wrist Drop -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Key clinical pearls in the evaluation of wrist drop include precise lesion localization through focused motor and sensory examination, supplemented by electrodiagnostic studies when indicated. Nerve conduction studies and EMG are particularly valuable for distinguishing radial neuropathy from mimicking conditions such as cervical radiculopathy or brachial plexopathy. Prognosis after wrist drop depends on the severity and mechanism of radial nerve injury, but is generally favorable.

Key clinical pearls in the evaluation of wrist drop include precise lesion localization through focused motor and sensory examination, supplemented by electrodiagnostic studies when indicated. Nerve conduction studies and EMG are particularly valuable for distinguishing radial neuropathy from mimicking conditions such as cervical radiculopathy or brachial plexopathy. title: Wrist Drop -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Recovery typically requires at least 2 to 4 months, even in mild cases, and patients should be informed of the expected timeline for neurologic improvement. Incomplete recovery or irreversible motor deficits may be addressed with tendon transfer procedures to enhance functional outcomes. Common pitfalls include misdiagnosis from incomplete neurologic examination, overreliance on pain-limited weakness to infer motor deficit, and failure to consider nontraumatic or systemic causes of radial nerve injury.

title: Wrist Drop -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Wrist drop arises from a broad range of etiologies and, if unrecognized or inadequately managed, can cause significant morbidity and long-term functional impairment. Optimal care requires a coordinated interprofessional healthcare team focused on timely diagnosis, appropriate management, and restoration of function. Most cases of radial nerve palsy are amenable to conservative management with wrist splinting and structured rehabilitation. Physical therapists maintain joint mobility, prevent contractures, and guide progressive strengthening during neurologic recovery. Occupational therapists optimize hand function, facilitate activities of daily living, and provide adaptive strategies or assistive devices as needed.
